items.q: In SQL, which datatype would be most appropriate for storing email addresses?
options: TEXT
CHAR(50)
NVARCHAR(MAX)
VARCHAR(255)
items.explain: **VARCHAR(255)** — emails vary in length, so a *variable*-length type avoids the padding waste of `CHAR(50)`, and 255 comfortably covers the practical maximum. `TEXT` and `NVARCHAR(MAX)` are for large blocks of prose; they are often stored off-page and frequently cannot be indexed normally, which matters because email is usually a lookup or `UNIQUE` column.

items.q: `INSERT INTO Employee(emp_id, emp_name) VALUES (101, 'Alice');` — the table has a `salary DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL` column with no default. What happens?
options: Insert succeeds, database assigns a default value automatically
Insert succeeds, salary is set to 0
Insert succeeds, salary is NULL
Insert fails due to the NOT NULL constraint
items.explain: An omitted column takes its **DEFAULT**, and with no default declared that is **NULL** — which the `NOT NULL` constraint rejects. The insert **fails**. Databases do *not* invent a zero: `NOT NULL` without `DEFAULT` makes the column effectively **mandatory in every INSERT**.

items.q: Which relational-algebra operation can reduce duplicates and schema size simultaneously?
options: Selection (σ)
Intersection (∩)
Aggregation (ℱ)
Projection (π)
items.explain: **Projection (π)** drops *columns* — that is the schema-size reduction — and because relations are **sets**, dropping columns can make formerly distinct rows identical, so duplicates are eliminated too. **Selection (σ)** drops rows but keeps the full schema. Only π does both at once.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a valid SQL numeric datatype?
options: DECIMAL(10,2)
NUMERIC(5)
FLOAT(10)
CHAR(10)
items.explain: **CHAR(10)** is a fixed-length **character** type, not numeric. `DECIMAL`/`NUMERIC` are exact fixed-point types; `FLOAT` is approximate floating-point.

items.q: `Orders` has `FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES Customers(customer_id) ON DELETE CASCADE`. What happens when a customer is deleted from `Customers`?
options: All orders for that customer are automatically deleted
The deletion fails due to the foreign key constraint
customer_id in Orders is set to NULL
Nothing happens to Orders
items.explain: **ON DELETE CASCADE** propagates the delete downward — every child row referencing the removed parent is **deleted too**. The other options describe the alternatives: `NO ACTION`/`RESTRICT` (deletion fails), `SET NULL`, and no referential action at all.

items.q: Mapping a binary 1:1 relationship R between entity types S and T where **both have partial participation**, using the foreign-key (2 relations) approach — where does the foreign key go?
options: A foreign key is not necessary; a separate relationship table is always preferred for partial participation
The foreign key must be placed in S, referencing T
The foreign key must be placed in T, referencing S
The foreign key can be placed in either S or T, referencing the other relation
items.explain: With **both sides partial**, neither side is the obviously better host, so the foreign key may go in **either** relation. The usual tie-breaker does not apply here: when *one* side has **total** participation you put the FK on **that** side, because then it can be declared `NOT NULL` and no nulls appear. Both partial means whichever side you choose will carry some nulls.

items.q: Which scenario best illustrates 'data' as distinct from 'information'?
options: A report showing student pass/fail percentages for each department
A list of student IDs, names and phone numbers, stored without any sorting or grouping
A dashboard showing average student attendance by department and semester
A pie chart visualizing student enrollment trends over five years
items.explain: **Raw, unorganised facts** = data. The other three have all been **processed, organised and given context** to support a decision — that makes them **information**. The giveaway phrase is *'without any sorting or grouping'*.

items.q: What is one major drawback of a file-processing system?
options: Faster data access
Data redundancy and inconsistency
Centralized control of data
Automatic enforcement of constraints
items.explain: **Data redundancy and inconsistency** is drawback #1 — the same fact duplicated across files, which wastes space and lets copies disagree. The other three options are **benefits of a DBMS**, i.e. exactly what file systems lack.

items.q: In a database system, atomicity ensures that:
options: A transaction executes completely or not at all, with no partial effects
Every value lies within its declared domain
Data is replicated across multiple servers
Data is accessed by one user at a time
items.explain: **Atomicity** = **all-or-nothing**. The debit-and-credit transfer either does both steps or neither; a crash midway is undone by **rollback**. Single-user access is *isolation*; domain checking is *integrity*; replication is unrelated.

items.q: Which scenario illustrates a misuse of a derived attribute in an ER model?
options: Storing age in the database while also storing date_of_birth
Calculating age from date_of_birth during query execution
Using current date to calculate years of service
Creating a view that computes a value on the fly
items.explain: **Storing** a derived value alongside its source is the misuse — `age` is a function of `date_of_birth` **and today's date**, so a stored copy is stale within a day. The other three all *derive at read time*, which is correct. Ramakrishnan & Gehrke name `age` explicitly as an example of poor design.

items.q: Which ALTER TABLE operation is NOT allowed if the table already contains data (and dependent objects exist)?
options: Renaming a table
Adding a CHECK constraint
Adding a new column with a DEFAULT value
Dropping a column that has dependent foreign keys
items.explain: **Dropping a column referenced by a foreign key** is refused — it would leave the dependent constraint pointing at nothing. You must drop the constraint first (or use `CASCADE` where supported). Adding a column with a default, renaming, and adding a `CHECK` all work on populated tables — though a `CHECK` will be **rejected if existing rows violate it**.

items.q: If relation A has tuples {1, 2, 3, 4} and relation B has {3, 4, 5, 6}, then **A − B** gives:
items.explain: **Set difference** keeps tuples in A that are **not** in B → **{1, 2}**. For reference: `A ∩ B` = {3,4}, `B − A` = {5,6}, `A ∪ B` = {1,2,3,4,5,6}. Both `−` and `∩` require the relations to be **union-compatible**.

items.q: The Division (÷) operation is most useful when we want to:
options: Find tuples related to at least one value in another relation
Remove duplicate tuples from a relation
Combine two relations with identical schemas
Find tuples related to ALL values in another relation
items.explain: **Division answers 'for all' queries** — *'students who have taken **every** course offered by the CS department'*, *'suppliers who supply **all** parts'*. The 'at least one' case is an ordinary join or semi-join; that contrast is the whole point of the operator.

items.q: When mapping a weak entity set A that depends on a strong entity set B, how is the primary key of A's relation schema formed?
options: It is the combination of the primary key of the identifying strong entity set B and the discriminator (partial key) of A
It is the primary key of the strong entity set B only
It consists solely of the discriminator of A
It is derived from a hash function of all attributes of A
items.explain: A weak entity has no key of its own — only a **partial key / discriminator** that distinguishes it *among the dependents of one owner*. So the primary key is **owner's PK + discriminator**. `Dependent(`**`Essn`**`, `**`Dependent_name`**`, Sex, Bdate)` is the canonical example: two employees may each have a dependent named 'Anna', and only the pair is unique.

items.q: Which best represents a unique benefit of a DBMS over traditional file systems when handling a university's student records?
options: Restricting access to data completely
Storing plain text student names and marks
Manual entry and tallying of records
Supporting multiple concurrent users while maintaining consistency
items.explain: **Controlled concurrent access** is the distinctive capability — files can store text too, and blocking all access is not a benefit. The DBMS lets registrars, faculty and students work simultaneously while **transactions and locking** keep the data correct.

items.q: Which problem occurs when multiple users access and modify data simultaneously without proper control?
options: Concurrent access anomalies
Data isolation
Integrity problems
Atomicity failure
items.explain: **Concurrent-access anomalies** — the classic being the **lost update**, where two clerks both read a ₹10,000 balance, deduct ₹500 and ₹100, and the last writer's value overwrites the other, leaving 9,500 or 9,900 instead of 9,400.

items.q: A DBMS provides a central information store primarily to:
options: Remove the need for any constraints
Increase redundancy
Minimise redundancy and allow changes to be made at a single point, ensuring consistency
Make queries slower but safer
items.explain: Centralising the store is the direct fix for **drawback #1**: it **minimises redundancy**, and because each fact lives in one place, an update happens **at a single spot** — so copies cannot drift out of agreement.

items.q: Which scenario most justifies adopting a **parallel** database architecture over a distributed one?
options: A news app that loads local headlines depending on a user's GPS location
A cloud-based game that stores player stats and friend lists
A government meteorology centre analysing real-time satellite data for cyclone predictions
A blogging platform used globally that stores content by region
items.explain: Meteorology is **one enormous computation that must go faster** — a tightly-coupled cluster with many cores and shared disk. The other three are about **data living in different places** (geography, regions, users), which is the **distributed** case. Tell: *compute-bound and central* → parallel; *location-bound and spread* → distributed.

items.q: `Employee(emp_id, emp_name, salary)`. Which statement increases salaries by 10% **only for employees earning less than 5000**?
options: UPDATE Employee SET salary = salary*1.1;
UPDATE Employee SET salary = salary*1.1 WHERE salary < 5000;
UPDATE Employee WHERE salary < 5000 SET salary = salary*1.1;
UPDATE Employee SET salary*1.1 WHERE salary < 5000;
items.explain: The syntax is **`UPDATE table SET col = expr WHERE condition`** — `SET` always precedes `WHERE`, and `SET` needs an **assignment** (`salary = salary*1.1`), not a bare expression. Option 1 is syntactically fine but updates **everyone**.

items.q: Given `Employee(EmpID, Name, DeptID, Salary)` and `Department(DeptID, DeptName)`, evaluate: `Temp ← σ(Salary>60000)(Employee)` then `Result ← π(Name, DeptName)(Temp ⋈ Department)`. What does Result contain?
options: All department names regardless of salary
Names of departments with average salary > 60000
Names of employees earning > 60000
Names of employees earning > 60000 and their department names
items.explain: Read it inside-out: **σ** filters employees earning over 60000, the **natural join** attaches each one's department row via the shared `DeptID`, and **π** keeps `Name` and `DeptName`. So: **high earners paired with their department names**. There is no aggregation anywhere, which rules out the 'average salary' option.

items.q: What happens if a row violates a CHECK constraint during INSERT or UPDATE?
options: The operation fails and an error is thrown
The database ignores the CHECK constraint
The row is inserted/updated but flagged as invalid
The row is automatically corrected to satisfy the constraint
items.explain: Constraints are **enforced, not advisory** — the statement **fails with an error** and the row is not written. A DBMS never silently 'corrects' your data; that would be a worse outcome than rejecting it, since it would hide the bug.

items.q: When is representing `phone_number` as a multivalued attribute (double ellipse) most appropriate?
options: When the phone number is derived from the department code
When all instructors have exactly one phone number
When the number of phone numbers per instructor varies
When phone numbers are the same for all instructors in a department
items.explain: A multivalued attribute exists exactly because an instructor may have **zero, one, or several** numbers, and **different instructors have different counts**. If everyone had exactly one it would be plain single-valued; a shared departmental number belongs on **Department**, not Instructor.

items.q: Given `emp_id INT PRIMARY KEY, emp_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, salary DECIMAL(10,2), join_date DATE DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE` — which is TRUE?
options: join_date cannot have a default value
emp_id can have duplicate values
emp_name can store NULL values
salary can store up to 10 digits in total, with 2 after the decimal point
items.explain: **`DECIMAL(p, s)`** = **precision** p (total significant digits) and **scale** s (digits after the point). So `DECIMAL(10,2)` holds **10 digits in total, 2 of them after the decimal** — a maximum of 99,999,999.99. Note the trap: the integer part gets p − s = **8** digits, not 10. `emp_name` is `NOT NULL`, `join_date` clearly *does* have a default, and a `PRIMARY KEY` forbids duplicates.

items.q: An attribute `PreviousDegrees` stores multiple tuples of (College, Year, Degree, Field). Which classification best fits?
options: Complex attribute
Redundant attribute
Multivalued attribute
Composite attribute
items.explain: It is **multivalued** (many degrees) **and composite** (four components each) — and the **nesting of the two is precisely what defines a complex attribute**. Written `{PreviousDegrees(College, Year, Degree, Field)}`: braces = multivalued, parentheses = composite.

items.q: Which correctly matches a schema level with its description?
options: Logical schema — Describes file storage techniques and indexing
View schema — Defines access-controlled subsets of data for different users
Subschema — Refers to low-level device-specific storage
Physical schema — Describes virtual views for users
items.explain: **View (external) schema** = the tailored, permission-bounded slice each user group sees. The distractors swap the pairs: *physical/internal* is storage and indexing, *logical/conceptual* is entities and relationships, and **'subschema' is an old synonym for external schema** — not a storage-level term.

items.q: Which indirectly helps reduce client-side computational burden in a two-tier architecture?
options: Disabling ODBC query translation
Moving data to local JSON files
Shifting SQL parsing and query execution to the server
Compiling JDBC drivers into the client program
items.explain: In client-server the **server does the parsing, optimisation and execution** and returns only the result set — so the client ships a short query string instead of processing data itself. Moving data to local files pushes work *back* onto the client; the other two do not change where computation happens.

items.q: What happens if you insert the string `'abc'` into a column defined as INT?
options: SQL stores 'abc' as NULL
SQL truncates 'abc' to 'a'
SQL automatically converts it to 0
SQL raises a data-type / conversion error
items.explain: This is **domain integrity** doing its job — the value is outside the column's declared domain, so the statement is **rejected with an error**. (Historical note: MySQL in its old non-strict mode *would* coerce to 0 with a warning; every modern default, including MySQL's `STRICT_TRANS_TABLES`, errors instead.)

items.q: Which most accurately represents a **relationship instance**?
options: A row in a table that links one specific instructor to one specific student
The set of all students in the 'Student' entity set
An attribute in the 'Course' entity
The 'advisor' diamond in an ER diagram
items.explain: An **instance** is one **specific association between named entities** — *Katz (45565) advises Shankar (12345)*. The **diamond** is the relationship **set/type** (the definition, part of the schema); the set of all students is an **entity set**.

items.q: A global supply chain suffers delays from poor visibility into inventory. Which database feature is most likely to resolve it?
options: Creating spreadsheet backups of inventory every week
Real-time synchronization of supplier and inventory tables across branches
Maintaining manual dispatch registers at warehouses
Triggering automatic email notifications
items.explain: The stated problem is **visibility** — branches cannot see each other's current state. **Real-time synchronization (a distributed database with replication)** fixes the cause. Weekly spreadsheets and manual registers recreate the **data-isolation** problem; email notifications treat the symptom.

items.q: Which most accurately reflects the definition of a database in a university context?
options: A set of spreadsheets with course names typed manually by different departments
A shared folder with scanned student mark sheets
A structured collection of interrelated student and course records maintained on a centralized server
A pile of physical student registration forms stored in an office
items.explain: The definition demands **related** data that is **logically coherent** and **built for a purpose**. Only option 3 has structure and interrelation; the others are unstructured collections — and the departmental spreadsheets are a textbook illustration of **redundancy and inconsistency**.

items.q: Which DDL command changes the datatype of a column in an existing table?
options: CHANGE TABLE ... COLUMN ...
MODIFY TABLE ... COLUMN ...
ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY COLUMN ...
UPDATE TABLE ... SET ...
items.explain: **`ALTER TABLE`** is the only DDL verb for changing structure; the sub-clause is `MODIFY COLUMN` in MySQL/Oracle and `ALTER COLUMN` in SQL Server/PostgreSQL. **`UPDATE` is DML** — it changes *values inside rows*, never the schema. That DDL-vs-DML distinction is the point of the question.

items.q: Which reflects an **indirect** responsibility of a DBA in maintaining system performance?
options: Designing user interface forms
Writing business logic in the application tier
Tuning index structures and access methods
Creating JavaScript front-end validators
items.explain: **Storage-structure and access-method definition** is a named DBA function — the DBA never writes the query, but by choosing **indexes** they change how fast everyone else's queries run. The other three belong to **application programmers**.

items.q: Owner–Property: each owner must own at least one property but can own many; each property must be owned by exactly one owner. Which (min, max) notation is correct?
options: Owner (0, N), Property (1, 1)
Owner (1, 1), Property (1, N)
Owner (0, 1), Property (1, N)
Owner (1, N), Property (1, 1)
items.explain: *'Must own at least one'* → Owner min = **1** (total participation); *'can own many'* → max = **N**. *'Owned by exactly one'* → Property is **(1, 1)**. Reading rule: the pair on a line constrains **the entity set that line attaches to**, counting how many relationship instances **each of its entities** joins.

items.q: What could be an indirect consequence if a DBA fails to periodically monitor disk space availability?
options: Transaction logs may overflow, causing system crashes
Logical schema changes become necessary
Query execution plans become invalid
Sophisticated users lose their access rights
items.explain: **Ensuring disk space availability** is listed under the DBA's *routine maintenance*. The subtle failure mode is the **transaction log**: it grows with every write, and if it cannot extend, the DBMS can no longer guarantee recovery — so it **refuses writes or halts**. The database can stop even when the *data* files have room.

items.q: `DELETE FROM Employee WHERE emp_id = 105;` and `Orders` has a foreign key to `Employee` with ON DELETE CASCADE. What happens?
options: Only employee 105 is deleted
Employee 105 and all related orders are deleted
Deletion fails because of the foreign key
Only orders are deleted, employee remains
items.explain: **CASCADE deletes downward** — the parent row goes, and every child row referencing it goes with it, in the same transaction. Note this can chain: if `Orders` itself has cascading children, those are removed too, which is why CASCADE deserves care in production schemas.

items.q: Which constraint ensures a column's values are unique but still allows NULL?
options: CHECK
PRIMARY KEY
UNIQUE
NOT NULL
items.explain: **UNIQUE** enforces distinctness but **permits NULL** — and because two NULLs are not considered equal, most systems allow **several** NULL rows. **PRIMARY KEY = UNIQUE + NOT NULL**, which is exactly the difference being tested here.

items.q: Which statement about Union (∪) and Difference (−) is true?
options: Union allows different attribute domains, but Difference does not
Difference can be applied to relations with different schemas
Union automatically removes duplicate tuples but Difference does not
Both operations require the relations to be union-compatible — same number of attributes with matching domains
items.explain: **∪, ∩ and − all require union-compatibility**: the same **degree** (number of attributes) and **compatible domains** position by position. (Attribute *names* need not match in the formal algebra — the domains must.) Beware the half-truth distractor claiming *union removes duplicates but difference does not* — **every** set operation removes duplicates, because relations are sets.

items.q: A `Product` entity has primary key `Product_ID` and a **multivalued** attribute `Color`. What is the correct relational schema?
options: Product (Product_ID, Color)
Product (Product_ID) and Product_Color (Product_ID, Color), with Product_ID a foreign key in Product_Color
Product (Product_ID, Color1, Color2, ...)
Product (Product_ID) and Color (Color_ID, Product_ID)
items.explain: **A multivalued attribute always becomes its own relation**, holding the owner's key plus the attribute, with **{Product_ID, Color} as the composite primary key** and Product_ID a foreign key. Option 1 breaks **1NF** (non-atomic values); option 3 hard-codes an arbitrary limit and is unqueryable.

items.q: A university wants to track which instructor supervises which student on which project. Why can't this be modelled with only binary relationships?
options: A set of binary relationships cannot express the three-way dependency simultaneously
The ER model doesn't support multiple relationships
It increases redundancy in course records
A student can only have one instructor
items.explain: A student may have **different instructors for different projects**. Split into three binary relationships, the pairs *(Asha, Rao)* and *(Asha, Iyer)* both exist and neither records **which project each applies to** — the three-way fact is **not the sum of its two-way projections**. Hence a ternary `proj_guide`.

items.q: What does `ρ E1(EmpID, EName, DNo) ( π EmpID, Name, DeptID (Employee) )` do?
options: Selects employees with a specific DeptID
Projects EmpID, Name and DeptID, then renames the result to E1 with attributes EmpID, EName, DNo
Joins Employee with a Dept relation
Deletes the attribute DeptID
items.explain: **ρ (rho) is rename.** The inner **π** picks three columns; ρ gives the result the relation name **E1** and renames its attributes positionally to `(EmpID, EName, DNo)`. Renaming matters for **self-joins** and for making relations union-compatible. No σ appears, so nothing is filtered.

items.q: Two instructors simultaneously update a student's grade. The system ensures correctness using:
options: Integrity constraints
View definition
Concurrency control and locking
Redundant backups
items.explain: Simultaneous writes to the same item is the **lost-update** hazard, prevented by **concurrency control (transactions + locking)**. Integrity constraints check *what values are legal*, not *what happens when two writers interleave* — a different axis entirely.

items.q: For an N-ary relationship type (N > 2) mapped to a new relation S, which is NOT a direct component of S?
options: The simple attributes of the N-ary relationship type
The simple components of composite attributes of the N-ary relationship type
The foreign-key attributes which are primary keys of the participating entity types
The derived attributes of any of the participating entity types
items.explain: An N-ary relationship relation gets: the **primary keys of all N participating entities** as foreign keys (together forming its key), plus the relationship's **own descriptive attributes**, with composites broken into simple components. **Derived attributes are never stored anywhere** — they are computed on demand, so they belong to no relation.

items.q: Which statement about DELETE is TRUE?
options: DELETE FROM Employee; removes all rows but keeps the table structure
DELETE cannot have a WHERE clause
DELETE automatically resets identity columns
DELETE FROM Employee; removes the table itself
items.explain: **DELETE is DML** — it removes **rows**, leaving the table, its columns and constraints intact. **`DROP TABLE`** removes the table itself. Contrast **`TRUNCATE`**: also empties the table but is DDL, is not row-by-row logged, cannot take a `WHERE`, and typically **does** reset identity counters.

items.q: Why might a company like Netflix rely on distributed databases rather than a centralized one?
options: To reduce the need for user authentication
To ensure low-latency access and personalized recommendations across global regions
To simplify billing operations across countries
To stream videos from a local device instead of the cloud
items.explain: Distributed databases place data **near the users who read it**, cutting latency, and add **replication** for fault tolerance. A single central server would force every request worldwide through one location — the exact problem distribution solves.

items.q: Which SELECT returns only distinct **combinations** of emp_name and salary?
options: SELECT emp_name, salary FROM Employee;
SELECT DISTINCT emp_name, salary FROM Employee;
SELECT DISTINCT emp_name FROM Employee;
SELECT emp_name, DISTINCT salary FROM Employee;
items.explain: **`DISTINCT` applies to the entire select list**, not to one column — so `DISTINCT emp_name, salary` de-duplicates **pairs**. Option 4 is a **syntax error**: `DISTINCT` may appear only once, immediately after `SELECT`.

items.q: What is the main difference between ON DELETE CASCADE and ON DELETE SET NULL?
options: Both set the child column to NULL
CASCADE deletes parent rows, SET NULL deletes child rows
CASCADE deletes the child rows, SET NULL sets the child's foreign-key column to NULL
Both delete child rows
items.explain: Both are **referential actions on the child** when a parent is deleted. **CASCADE** removes the child rows; **SET NULL** keeps them but **orphans them by nulling the FK column** — which naturally requires that column to be nullable, so it cannot be used where the FK is `NOT NULL` or part of the primary key.

items.q: In min–max notation (1, N), what does the number 1 represent?
options: Relationship type
Key attribute
Maximum participation
Minimum participation
items.explain: In **(min, max)** the first number is the **minimum** — and `min = 1` means **total participation** (every entity must take part at least once). `min = 0` means partial. The second number caps the **maximum**.

items.q: In an ER model, a weak entity must always have:
options: A partial key (discriminator) and an identifying relationship with its owner
A composite primary key of its own
At least one derived attribute
A multivalued attribute
items.explain: A weak entity has **no key of its own**. It needs a **partial key / discriminator** — unique only among one owner's dependents — plus an **identifying relationship** to the owner, and it has **total participation** in that relationship. In diagrams: double rectangle, double diamond, dashed-underlined partial key.

items.q: A foreign-key constraint is added to the relational schema of a weak entity set. What is its primary purpose?
options: To define the primary key of the weak entity
To ensure that for each tuple representing a weak entity there is a corresponding tuple representing the identifying strong entity
To enforce uniqueness across all attributes in the weak entity's schema
To establish a many-to-many relationship between the weak and strong entity
items.explain: This is **referential integrity** enforcing the weak entity's **existence dependency** — a dependent cannot exist without its employee. Note the owner's key does double duty: it is **part of** the weak entity's primary key *and* a **foreign key**, but those are two separate constraints, and the FK is the one guaranteeing the owner exists.

items.q: Which of the following is an entity with **conceptual** rather than physical existence?
options: A server rack
A library book
A university course
A delivery van
items.explain: A **course** is abstract — you cannot touch it, yet it has identity and attributes. Companies, jobs, projects and reservations are the other standard examples. Both concrete and abstract things serve equally as entities; assuming entities must be physical is a common modelling error.

items.q: A DBA adds an index to speed up a slow report. No application code changes. Which property made this possible?
options: Atomicity
Entity integrity
Logical data independence
Physical data independence
items.explain: An index is a **physical/internal schema** object. Changing it without touching the logical schema or applications is **physical data independence**, delivered by the **conceptual/internal mapping**. Logical independence would be adding or removing a *column* without breaking applications — much harder to achieve.

items.q: You run `INSERT` 500 times, then `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN`. Which changed the schema, and which changed the state?
options: The INSERTs changed the state; the ALTER changed the schema
The INSERTs changed the schema; the ALTER changed the state
Both changed the schema
Both changed the state
items.explain: **Schema = the design** (≈ variable declarations + types); **state = the data at a moment** (≈ the variables' values). **DML (`INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE`) changes state**; **DDL (`CREATE`/`ALTER`/`DROP`) changes schema**. Many states correspond to one schema.

items.q: In the database design process, which phase produces a schema that is still **DBMS-independent**?
options: Logical design (data model mapping)
Conceptual design
Transaction implementation
Physical design
items.explain: The dashed line in the design diagram falls **between conceptual and logical design**. The **conceptual schema** (your ER diagram) is DBMS-independent; the **logical schema** is expressed in the data model of a *specific* DBMS. This is what lets you argue about the business without MySQL's limitations entering the discussion.

items.q: Which DBMS module reads the system catalog to choose an efficient execution plan?
options: The pre-compiler
The DDL compiler
The query optimizer
The stored data manager
items.explain: The **DDL compiler writes** metadata into the catalog; the **query optimizer reads** it — statistics, indexes, column types — to pick a plan. That write-once/read-many asymmetry is the **self-describing nature** rendered as a wiring diagram, and it is why a schema change can invalidate a cached plan.

items.q: In a `Student —Enrolls— Course` relationship, where does the `Grade` attribute belong?
options: In both Student and Course
In the Student entity
In the Course entity
As a descriptive attribute on the Enrolls relationship
items.explain: A grade only exists **once a student and a course are connected**, so it is a **descriptive attribute** — an oval on the **diamond**. The test: *does the value exist for the entity on its own, or only for the pair?* Same logic puts `hours` on `works_on` and a manager's `start_date` on `manages`.

items.q: Which relationship requires **explicit role names** in the ER diagram?
options: Course — prereq — Course
Instructor — advisor — Student
Employee — works_on — Project
Student — Enrolls — Course
items.explain: **`prereq` is recursive** — the *same* entity set appears at both ends, so the two lines are indistinguishable without labels like `course_id` and `prereq_id`. The pair `(CS201, CS101)` is meaningless until you know which end is the prerequisite. Roles are optional when the entity sets differ, **mandatory** when they don't.

items.q: A **1:N** relationship between `Department` (one) and `Employee` (many) is reduced to relations. What is the correct result?
options: A new relation holding both primary keys
The Department key becomes a foreign key in Employee
The Employee key becomes a foreign key in Department
Both relations are merged into one
items.explain: For **1:N**, the key of the **'one' side** is posted as a **foreign key on the 'many' side** — each employee stores its single `Dnumber`. No extra table is needed. Only **M:N** requires its own relation; the reverse placement is impossible because a department would need many employee keys in one column.

items.q: An ER diagram shows the `CAR` entity with **two** underlined attributes: `VIN` and `VehicleTagNumber(Number, State)`. What does this mean?
options: The two attributes together form one composite key
The diagram contains an error — only one key may be underlined
CAR has two candidate keys; one must be chosen as primary key when reducing to relational
VIN is the primary key and VehicleTagNumber is a foreign key
items.explain: In an **ER diagram every key is underlined**, so two underlines legitimately mean **two candidate keys**. (In a **relational schema** only the single chosen **primary key** is underlined.) It also shows a key may be **composite** — a plate number alone is not unique across states.

items.q: A bank runs two systems: one handles ATM withdrawals; the other analyses five years of transactions to score loan applicants. Which pair correctly labels them?
options: Both are OLAP
Both are OLTP
ATM = OLAP, loan scoring = OLTP
ATM = OLTP, loan scoring = OLAP
items.explain: **OLTP** = many users, **small** reads and writes that must finish in milliseconds — the ATM. **OLAP** = few, **enormous** scans that build predictive models — loan scoring, one of the named examples. The two want opposite physical designs, which is why banks usually run them on separate systems.

items.q: Which constraint pair is required to guarantee **entity integrity** on a table?
options: PRIMARY KEY (which implies UNIQUE + NOT NULL)
FOREIGN KEY and NOT NULL
DEFAULT and CHECK
UNIQUE and CHECK
items.explain: **Entity integrity** = every row is uniquely identifiable, so the primary key must be **unique** *and* **never null** — exactly what `PRIMARY KEY` enforces. A bare `UNIQUE` column still permits NULLs, which is why it alone is not enough. `FOREIGN KEY` provides **referential** integrity, a different guarantee.
